lesson.title: Fuel Meets Oxygen: Inside Combustion Reactions
lesson.summary: Combustion reactions are fast, energy releasing reactions between a fuel and oxygen gas, and for hydrocarbon fuels the products are reliably carbon dioxide and water.
lesson.body:
The Reaction Types Overview introduced combustion as one of the core reaction families, and Chemical Changes taught you the signs that a true chemical transformation has taken place: new substances form, and energy is released or absorbed, often as heat and light. Combustion is the reaction family where those signs are the most dramatic. In a combustion reaction, a fuel reacts rapidly with oxygen gas, O2, breaking and reforming bonds in a way that releases a large amount of energy very quickly, which is why combustion shows up as flame, heat, and often light.

For hydrocarbon fuels, compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen, sometimes with oxygen already included, like sugars or alcohols, complete combustion follows a reliable pattern: the fuel reacts with enough O2 to convert every carbon atom into carbon dioxide, CO2, and every hydrogen atom into water, H2O. This makes hydrocarbon combustion equations very predictable to balance, since you always know the products before you start.

Consider the combustion of propane, the fuel used in many gas grills and camping stoves: C3H8(g) + 5 O2(g) -> 3 CO2(g) + 4 H2O(g). To confirm this is balanced, count atoms on each side. Carbon: 3 in C3H8 on the left, 3 in 3 CO2 on the right. Hydrogen: 8 in C3H8 on the left, 4 times 2 equals 8 in 4 H2O on the right. Oxygen: 5 times 2 equals 10 oxygen atoms on the left, and on the right 3 CO2 contributes 3 times 2 equals 6 oxygens while 4 H2O contributes 4 oxygens, for a total of 6 plus 4 equals 10. Every element balances, so the coefficients 1, 5, 3, 4 are correct.

Combustion is not limited to hydrocarbons. Reactive metals also combust when heated in the presence of oxygen, for example burning magnesium ribbon: 2 Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2 MgO(s). The pattern is the same in spirit: a substance reacts with O2 and releases a burst of energy, here as the intense white light magnesium is known for. It is also worth knowing that combustion is only complete when there is enough oxygen available to fully convert all the carbon to CO2. If oxygen is limited, incomplete combustion can occur instead, producing carbon monoxide, CO, or even soot, solid carbon, along with water, which is both less efficient and, in the case of carbon monoxide, dangerous. Combustion reactions like propane's will reappear later as convenient examples once you start doing quantitative stoichiometry calculations, since their products are so predictable.
